items.followUp: Define the efficiency of a machine and calculate it if the useful output energy is 600 J and the input energy is 800 J.

rubric.why: The definition must identify efficiency as a comparison of useful output with input.
rubric.description: Defines efficiency as useful output divided by input.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that efficiency is the ratio of useful output to input (work or energy).

rubric.why: The formula expresses efficiency as a percentage of the input that becomes useful output.
rubric.description: Writes the percentage formula for efficiency.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct formula, such as efficiency = (useful output ÷ input) × 100%.

modelAnswer: The efficiency of a system is the ratio of its useful output to its input.
Efficiency = (useful output ÷ input) × 100%.

items.followUp: A barometer contains mercury. State why mercury is more suitable than water for measuring atmospheric pressure.

rubric.why: Water's low density means a much greater column height is needed to balance atmospheric pressure.
rubric.description: Identifies water's low density.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that water is less dense than mercury.

rubric.why: A water barometer would need an impractically tall column, about 10.3 m high.
rubric.description: Explains the impractical height of a water column.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for noting that the water column would be about 10.3 m (or roughly 10 m) high.

modelAnswer: Water has a low density compared with mercury.
Therefore, a water barometer would need a column about 10.3 m high, which is impractical.

rubric.why: The conversion from kelvin to Celsius requires subtracting 273.
rubric.description: Uses the correct conversion relation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for writing °C = K − 273 (or an equivalent relation).

rubric.why: Subtracting 273 from 300 K gives 27°C.
rubric.description: Gives the converted temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct answer, 27°C.

modelAnswer: Given: T = 300 K
Temperature in Celsius = T(K) − 273
Temperature in Celsius = 300 − 273
Temperature = 27°C

items.followUp: Define heat capacity and state its SI unit.

rubric.why: Heat capacity describes the heat needed to raise the temperature of a whole body by one kelvin.
rubric.description: Defines heat capacity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it is the heat required to raise a body's temperature by 1 K.

rubric.why: The SI unit follows from energy divided by temperature change.
rubric.description: Gives the SI unit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for J K⁻¹ (or J/K).

modelAnswer: Heat capacity is the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of a body by 1 K.
Its SI unit is joule per kelvin (J K⁻¹).

items.followUp: Derive the second equation of motion, s = ut + ½at², using a speed-time graph.

rubric.why: Displacement is the area under the speed-time graph, a trapezium.
rubric.description: Writes displacement as the area under the graph.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for s = ½(u + v)t.

rubric.why: The first equation of motion supplies the relation between final speed and time.
rubric.description: Uses the first equation of motion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for v = u + at or its rearranged equivalent.

rubric.why: Substitution of v = u + at into the graph-area equation leads to the required expression.
rubric.description: Substitutes for v and simplifies the expression.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct substitution and simplification to s = ut + ½at².

rubric.why: The final equation is the result of the derivation.
rubric.description: States the third equation of motion correctly.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the final result s = ut + ½at².

modelAnswer: From the speed-time graph, displacement is the area of the trapezium: s = ½(u + v)t.
Using the first equation of motion, v = u + at.
Substitute v = u + at into the displacement equation: s = ½(u + u + at)t.
Therefore, s = ½(2u + at)t = ut + ½at².

items.followUp: Define potential energy and derive the expression for the potential energy of a body raised through height h.

rubric.why: Potential energy is associated with a body's position or configuration.
rubric.description: Defines potential energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining it as energy possessed due to position or configuration.

rubric.why: A suitable example illustrates stored energy due to position.
rubric.description: Gives an example of potential energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a relevant example, such as a raised body or water stored at a height.

rubric.why: The force that must be overcome in raising the body is its weight.
rubric.description: Identifies the force against which work is done.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the lifting force is the body's weight, mg.

rubric.why: Work done in raising the body through height h is stored as potential energy.
rubric.description: Derives the potential-energy expression.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for using work = force × distance and obtaining PE = mgh.

modelAnswer: Potential energy is the energy possessed by a body due to its position or configuration.
For example, a body raised above the ground has potential energy.
To raise a body of mass m through height h, work is done against its weight: F = mg.
Work done = force × distance = mgh.
This work is stored as potential energy; therefore, PE = mgh.

items.followUp: A perpendicular force of 80 N acts on a spanner 0.25 m from a nut. Calculate the torque.

rubric.why: The applied force is given in the question.
rubric.description: Identifies the applied force.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for recording F = 100 N.

rubric.why: The distance must be converted from centimetres to metres for SI substitution.
rubric.description: Converts the moment arm to SI units.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for recording the perpendicular distance as 0.10 m.

rubric.why: Torque is the product of force and perpendicular distance from the pivot.
rubric.description: Writes the torque formula.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for torque = force × perpendicular distance.

rubric.why: Correct substitution gives the torque in newton-metres.
rubric.description: Substitutes the values into the formula.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct substitution, such as τ = 100 × 0.10.

rubric.why: The calculated torque is 10 N m.
rubric.description: Gives the answer with the correct unit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for 10 N m.

modelAnswer: Given: F = 100 N; r = 10 cm = 0.10 m
Formula: τ = F × r
Substitution: τ = 100 N × 0.10 m
τ = 10 N m

items.followUp: A steel wire 2 m long with cross-sectional area 4 × 10⁻⁵ m² extends by 2 mm under a force of 8,000 N. Calculate its Young's modulus.

rubric.why: The given values, including extension in SI units, are needed for the calculation.
rubric.description: Records the data and converts extension to metres.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the given quantities and converting 1 mm to 1 × 10⁻³ m.

rubric.why: Young's modulus is defined as stress divided by strain.
rubric.description: Writes the Young's modulus relation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for Y = stress/strain.

rubric.why: Substituting stress = F/A and strain = ΔL/L gives the working formula.
rubric.description: Rearranges to a formula using force, length, area, and extension.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for Y = FL/(AΔL).

rubric.why: The SI values yield a modulus of 2 × 10¹¹ Pa.
rubric.description: Substitutes the values and obtains the numerical result.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correct SI substitution and calculation.

rubric.why: Young's modulus is a pressure, so its SI unit is pascal.
rubric.description: States the final answer with unit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for 2 × 10¹¹ Pa.

modelAnswer: Given: L = 1 m; A = 5 × 10⁻⁵ m²; F = 10,000 N; ΔL = 1 mm = 1 × 10⁻³ m
Young's modulus: Y = stress ÷ strain
Y = (F/A) ÷ (ΔL/L) = FL/(AΔL)
Substitution: Y = (10,000 N × 1 m) ÷ (5 × 10⁻⁵ m² × 1 × 10⁻³ m)
Y = 2 × 10¹¹ N/m² = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa
